title: Gob plugin
description: This plugin was created to allow parsing of Go language created gob stream. gob streams are created using the Go gob package. This package is used to serialize Go types into binary streams. The documentation for the gob package can be found at: https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/gob.

Your heuristic dissector is creating a conversation for every packet it looks at, and allocating a gob data structure for it, before it decides whether it has any gob data.

At a minimum, these steps should be pushed after the `gob_validate()` check. It's unusual to do it in the heuristic at all; usually you'd create the conversation in your main dissector (`dissect_gob_stream()` in this case).

You don't appear to be using the converation data outside of this heuristic function at all. Even within this function, whatever previous conversation data you fetch gets unconditionally overwritten by the call to `gob_validate()` anyway so there doesn't seem to be a point in storing and fetching it. What is your intent here?

If you're trying to use conversations to strengthen the heuristic for streams of smaller packets, then you should look into `conversation_set_dissector()`. You can call that without even needing protocol-specific conversation data. Look at how other dissectors use it before you add it; in particular, you should check for an existing per-conversation dissector first and not override it unless you're really sure.

After a discussion with David, although it looks like the current code works, the use of conversation_set_dissector may simplify the workflow. David was right to state that the reason for the logic is to avoid false positives on smaller packets. Our intent is to only accept gob objects with no type specifications if we have seen gob objects with type specifications earlier in the stream. The current code tries to store this state in the conversation proto_data. I will explore if we can instead always fail validation for gob objects with no type specification, but set the dissector for the conversation to gob as soon as we see a gob object with some type specification. This way, the heuristic does not need to be invoked anymore on future packets for the same stream. This would allow us to avoid small positives on small packets without requiring to allocate memory to store conversation state information.
I have removed the code to keep track of the state inside a conversation and call the conversation_set_dissector instead when we detect a type specification in the first gob stream of a TCP stream.

According to [its documentation](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/ca6a8b7eff51bf32b9a880a4830c8059dd084a05/epan/dissectors/packet-tcp.h#L131), `tcp_dissect_pdus()` is intended for PDUs with a fixed-size header which contains enough information to determine the length of the rest of the PDU. The idea is that Wireshark can use it to tell how long of a message to expect, even if it's fragmented across several packets, and reassemble those packets to get the full message.

You're calling it with 0 as the size of the header, which is an early sign that you may be mis-applying the function. Your get-length function (`gob_get_stream_length()`, via `gob_get_message_length()`) appears to work by just walking the entire tvbuff, so it will probably fail to identify a gob stream that's longer than one packet anyway.

I suggest you take a look at [section 2.7 of `README.dissector`](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/ca6a8b7eff51bf32b9a880a4830c8059dd084a05/doc/README.dissector#L3329).

Based on how your dissector shows the data, it appears as though there is a leading length field for any type definitions that may be present, and another leading length field at the start of the data block. If this is accurate, then you could write a different `gob_get_message_length()` function which figures out the type definition length, and tries to skip ahead that many bytes to find the data block length. If the TVB doesn't have that much data, then your function can return 0 to indicate it needs more packets before it can determine the full message length. Otherwise, it can combine the values of the two length fields and return the total expected length of the message. Either way, the function doesn't need to parse the complete message, nor even *have* a complete message, to calculate how long it will be.

If this approach can work, then the size of the "fixed header" could be as small as the largest number of bytes needed to make up a gob-flavoured varint, instead of being 0. Like I said, your function can return 0 if it needs more bytes in order to calculate the full length, and it will be called again with a larger TVB once it has more data.

Otherwise, if I've misinterpreted and there's really no way to know how big a message will be until you have the whole thing, then you won't be able to use `tcp_dissect_pdus()` at all, and you'll have to investigate the approach described in section 2.7.2 of `README.dissector`.

The gob_get_message_length invoked gob_get_stream_length which was returning 0 if the tvb did not contain enough of the gob stream to determine the length. However, gob_get_stream_length had a few logic issues, which I have fixed, and also, passing 0 as the size of the header was wrong. The length is expected to be 1 byte most times, so setting the header to 1 is good enough. If it happens to be greater than 1, the current gob deserialization code will be able to detect and adjust accordingly. The new gob_get_stream_length is now able to handle having more than one gob stream in a single pakcet and having a gib stream than spans multiple packets.
You shouldn't alter the column headers before you know that there will be gob data in the packet. These calls should be moved down past any of your checks which could `return 0`.

The overall approach of this code appears to be a two-step process of fully parsing an entire gob stream first, and then rewinding and using that information to produce the actual dissection. Is that a correct assessment?

What you have here seems to work, and I don't think gob is a common enough serialization format for me to demand you change the approach. But it's not a typical paradigm for Wireshark dissectors, especially for messages that can span several packets.

It's generally better for the code to dissect what it sees, as it sees it, packet by packet. That makes it more robust by allowing partial dissection of an incomplete message, e.g. if the capture was stopped before the end of the gob message was received.

It also makes it more likely that your heuristic will successfully identify and parse a gob stream that crosses multiple packets. Your current heuristic appears to walk the full message; if it could be reasonably sure that a single packet looks like the start of a gob stream, then it can start by dissecting that packet, and use `conversation_set_dissector()` to tell Wireshark to come back to your full dissector when it has more packets from that stream.

It can still build up information about the protocol (such as the type definitions) as it reads each fragment, so that later parts can draw on that information. That's the intended use of conversation data.

It also feels like overkill for your code to fully parse the gob structure in a way that allows arbitrary access to any part of it, disconnected from its presence in the packet data. Dissectors usually show how the bytes would be interpreted, but don't fully parse them, if that makes any sense — to use another example, the JSON dissector shows the keys and values it sees as it sees them, but it doesn't hold the JSON structure in memory. 

Like I said, your approach will probably be okay, even if it does break the mold. But we'll have to keep in mind that this has been handled in this way, in case problems appear down the road for users who do see a lot of gob traffic.

+    # Unfortunately unable to use Wireshark-defined fixtures (like dirs) as they are not

+        basename = capture_file.name.split(".")[0]
